top_choice_rationale: Anne Carson (P002) is my first choice on voice, formal and linguistic achievement, and sustained imaginative depth. Her voice is recognisable at the level of the line. From general public knowledge, Autobiography of Red, Eros the Bittersweet, the lyric and essay collections, and Nox suggest recurring concerns (desire, loss, the pull of the ancient text, the fragment as a unit of thought) that return across changing forms. I read this as a method with a core, not as a run of one-off experiments. I would rest the citation on original poetry, essay and hybrid narrative, leave translations and adaptations out as a ground, and not rest it on book-design effects in Nox. The margin over Cărtărescu (P001) is narrow, and I rank him second without reservation about his architectural ambition. The difference is a judgment about weighting, line-level economy and formal range against sustained large-scale construction, and the files do not settle it. My main uncertainties are whether Carson's hybrid forms are a durable core or a narrower erudite mode, and whether her later volumes hold up. I have not read the full corpus or verified any source. Translation limits affect every shortlisted writer, so they do not separate the two. The fact that Carlberg and I both prefer Carson is not evidence of merit. If readers of the Romanian found real development in Cărtărescu's late novels, or readers of Carson's later volumes found only an erudite mode, I would reconsider. A prize to either writer is preferable to no award (P000), which I rank last because both proposals rest on substantial, distinctive oeuvres.
